claim: Working memory enables us to bridge past sensory information to upcoming future behaviour.
source: Working memory enables us to bridge past sensory information to upcoming future behaviour.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about working memory function that draws from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Working memory is concerned with two components: the past and the future.
source: Accordingly, by its very nature, working memory is concerned with two components: the past and the future.
evidence: This is a conceptual claim based on logical inference from the nature of working memory.

claim: In conventional laboratory tasks, past and future components of working memory are often conflated.
source: Yet, in conventional laboratory tasks, these two components are often conflated, such as when sensory information in working memory is encoded and tested at the same location.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of existing experimental paradigms in the field.

claim: The task dissociated the past (encoded location) and future (to-be-tested location) attributes of visual contents in working memory.
source: We developed a task in which we dissociated the past (encoded location) and future (to-be-tested location) attributes of visual contents in working memory.
evidence: This describes the experimental design implemented in the study.

claim: Past and future memory attributes can be independently tracked through gaze during mnemonic selection.
source: This enabled us to independently track the utilisation of past and future memory attributes through gaze, as observed during mnemonic selection.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: The results reveal joint consideration of past and future locations.
source: Our results reveal the joint consideration of past and future locations.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Joint consideration of past and future locations was prevalent even at the single-trial level of individual saccades.
source: This was prevalent even at the single-trial level of individual saccades that were jointly biased to the past and future.
evidence: This is a key finding supported by single-trial analysis of saccade data.

claim: Both past and future memory attributes are retained and can be accessed together when memory contents become relevant for behaviour.
source: This uncovers the rich nature of working memory representations, whereby both past and future memory attributes are retained and can be accessed together when memory contents become relevant for behaviour.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Working memory is a fundamental cognitive function that enables us to hold onto past sensory information in service of upcoming future behaviour.
source: Working memory is a fundamental cognitive function that enables us to hold onto past sensory information in service of upcoming future behaviour (D'Esposito and Postle, 2015; van Ede and Nobre, 2023; Rainer et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In dynamic everyday situations, sensory information often disappears at one specific location but becomes relevant at another location.
source: By contrast, in the dynamic situations we face every day, sensory information often disappears at one specific location (where it enters visual working memory) but becomes relevant at another location (as also in Brincat et al., 2021; Doherty et al., 2005; Woodman et al., 2012; Kahneman et al., 1992; Zaksas et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies and general knowledge about real-world scenarios.

claim: Twenty-five human volunteers performed the working-memory task.
source: Twenty-five human volunteers performed a working-memory task in which visual memory items were encoded and tested at different locations (Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes the sample size and basic experimental procedure.

claim: Participants memorised two coloured gratings with different orientations presented either vertically or horizontally.
source: Participants memorised two coloured gratings with different orientations presented either vertically or horizontally.
evidence: This describes the experimental stimuli and procedure.

claim: Memory content was always tested in the orthogonal axis at a predictable location.
source: The crucial manipulation was that we always tested memory content in the orthogonal axis and at a predictable location (depending on the future rule that we varied across sessions; see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for the four possible rules).
evidence: This describes a key aspect of the experimental design.

claim: Participants were able to perform the dynamic visual working-memory task with an average accuracy of 70±2 percent correct.
source: Participants were able to perform this dynamic visual working-memory task, with an average accuracy of 70±2percent correct (mean ± SEM) and an average reaction time of 1218±125 ms.
evidence: This reports behavioral performance data from the experiment.

claim: The average reaction time was 1218±125 ms.
source: Participants were able to perform this dynamic visual working-memory task, with an average accuracy of 70±2percent correct (mean ± SEM) and an average reaction time of 1218±125 ms.
evidence: This reports behavioral performance data from the experiment.

claim: Directional biases in saccades have previously been shown to be sensitive to selective spatial attention.
source: Specifically, we focused on directional biases in saccades, that have previously been shown to be sensitive to selective spatial attention (Engbert and Kliegl, 2003; Hafed and Clark, 2002; Rolfs, 2009; Laubrock et al., 2010; Yuval-Greenberg et al., 2014; Shelchkova and Poletti, 2020; Fernández et al., 2023; Lowet et al., 2018), even when directed internally (Liu et al., 2022a; van Ede et al., 2021; van Ede et al., 2019; van Ede et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: After cue onset, saccades became biased in the direction of the encoded (past) location of the selected memorized target.
source: As shown in Figure 1b, after cue onset, saccades became biased in the direction of the encoded (past) location of the selected memorized target, as demonstrated by significantly more gaze shifts toward vs. away from the encoded location of the target (Figure 1b; cluster p<0.001), starting from around 200 ms after the cue.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis of eye-tracking data.

claim: The bias toward the past location started from around 200 ms after the cue.
source: As shown in Figure 1b, after cue onset, saccades became biased in the direction of the encoded (past) location of the selected memorized target, as demonstrated by significantly more gaze shifts toward vs. away from the encoded location of the target (Figure 1b; cluster p<0.001), starting from around 200 ms after the cue.
evidence: This temporal finding is supported by time-resolved analysis of the data.

claim: The retention of items in working memory continues to rely on their past encoded locations, even if items are known to become relevant at another location.
source: In our current task, this uniquely reveals how the retention of items in working memory continues to rely on their past encoded locations, even if items are known to become relevant (tested) at another location.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: A similar saccade bias to the relevant future location was found.
source: In contrast, as shown in Figure 1c and d, we found a similar saccade bias to the relevant future location (Figure 1c; cluster p<0.001).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis of eye-tracking data.

claim: The future bias emerged early after the cue.
source: Strikingly, this future bias also emerged early after the cue.
evidence: This temporal finding is supported by the data analysis.

claim: Past and future locations were considered at overlapping time windows.
source: An overlay of the spatial biases (toward vs. away) in the orthogonally manipulated past and future axes (Figure 1d), revealed consideration of past and future locations at overlapping time windows.
evidence: This finding is supported by comparison of temporal patterns in the data.

claim: Gaze biases in both axes were driven predominantly by microsaccades.
source: Gaze biases in both axes were driven predominantly by microsaccades (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and occurred similarly in horizontal-to-vertical and vertical-to-horizontal trials (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This finding is supported by analysis of saccade magnitude shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Gaze biases occurred similarly in horizontal-to-vertical and vertical-to-horizontal trials.
source: Gaze biases in both axes were driven predominantly by microsaccades (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and occurred similarly in horizontal-to-vertical and vertical-to-horizontal trials (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This finding is supported by separate analysis of different trial types.

claim: The past bias was relatively transient.
source: Moreover, while the past bias was relatively transient, the future bias continued to increase in anticipation of the test stimulus and increasingly incorporated eye movements beyond the microsaccade range (see Figure 1—figure supplement 4 for a more extended time range).
evidence: This temporal pattern is supported by extended time-range analysis.

claim: The future bias continued to increase in anticipation of the test stimulus and increasingly incorporated eye movements beyond the microsaccade range.
source: Moreover, while the past bias was relatively transient, the future bias continued to increase in anticipation of the test stimulus and increasingly incorporated eye movements beyond the microsaccade range (see Figure 1—figure supplement 4 for a more extended time range).
evidence: This finding is supported by magnitude and temporal analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: It is notoriously hard to disentangle the single-trial interpretation of averaged data.
source: While it is notoriously hard to disentangle the single-trial interpretation of averaged data (Stokes and Spaak, 2016), we were here able to do so by interrogating the individual saccade characteristics for which the two alternative scenarios make different predictions.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The majority of first-detected microsaccades were made toward the past and toward the future.
source: As shown in Figure 2a, the majority of first-detected microsaccades in our window of interest were made toward the past (right >left) and toward the future (top >bottom), replicating our prior analyses.
evidence: This finding is supported by analysis of saccade directions shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The past bias is particularly pronounced for saccades that also have a future bias.
source: In both cases, we see a clear dependency: the past bias is particularly pronounced for saccades that also have a future bias (Figure 2b) and, vice versa, the future bias is most pronounced for saccades that also have a past bias (Figure 2c).
evidence: This dependency is demonstrated by the single-saccade analysis shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The future bias is most pronounced for saccades that also have a past bias.
source: In both cases, we see a clear dependency: the past bias is particularly pronounced for saccades that also have a future bias (Figure 2b) and, vice versa, the future bias is most pronounced for saccades that also have a past bias (Figure 2c).
evidence: This dependency is demonstrated by the single-saccade analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: There was a clear interaction whereby the bias toward the future location was exclusively observed for those saccades that were also biased toward the past location.
source: We found a clear interaction (F(1, 24)=18.1, p<0.001, partial η2=0.43), whereby the bias toward the future location was exclusively observed for those saccades that were also biased toward the past location.
evidence: This interaction is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) of the binarized saccade data.

claim: There was no difference in future bias for saccades that were away from the past.
source: Indeed, follow-up t-tests revealed no difference in future bias for saccades that were away from the past (t(24) = 1.13, PBonferroni=1, d=0.23), but a clear future effect for saccades that were toward the past (t(24)=4.65, PBonferroni<0.001, d=0.93).
evidence: This finding is supported by post-hoc statistical testing.

claim: There was a clear future effect for saccades that were toward the past.
source: Indeed, follow-up t-tests revealed no difference in future bias for saccades that were away from the past (t(24) = 1.13, PBonferroni=1, d=0.23), but a clear future effect for saccades that were toward the past (t(24)=4.65, PBonferroni<0.001, d=0.93).
evidence: This finding is supported by post-hoc statistical testing.

claim: The findings provide single-trial-level support for the truly joint consideration of past and future memory attributes.
source: This provides single-trial-level support with the truly joint consideration of past and future memory attributes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the single-saccade analysis results.

claim: The study unveils a novel, fundamental property of working memory – the joint availability and utilisation of past and future memory attributes.
source: Here, we brought the study of visual working memory into a dynamic context by experimentally dissociating (orthogonalising) the past (last-seen location) and future (to-be-tested location) attributes of visual memory contents, and independently tracking the utilisation of these two attributes through the gaze. Doing so, we unveil a novel, fundamental property of working memory – the joint availability and utilisation (i.e. selection) of past and future memory attributes.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The data provide key support for the proposal that memory is fundamentally future-oriented.
source: As such, our data provide key support for the proposal that memory is fundamentally future-oriented (van Ede and Nobre, 2023; Rainer et al., 1999; Nobre and Stokes, 2019; Schacter et al., 2007), while also reminding us that past memory attributes are not forgotten, even when these do not become relevant again.
evidence: This interpretation connects the findings to theoretical proposals in the literature.

claim: Past memory attributes are not forgotten, even when these do not become relevant again.
source: As such, our data provide key support for the proposal that memory is fundamentally future-oriented (van Ede and Nobre, 2023; Rainer et al., 1999; Nobre and Stokes, 2019; Schacter et al., 2007), while also reminding us that past memory attributes are not forgotten, even when these do not become relevant again.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding that past locations continue to be represented.

claim: Memory contents could have directly been remapped to their future-relevant location.
source: First, memory contents could have directly been remapped (Brincat et al., 2021; de Vries and van Ede, 2024; Hayhoe and Ballard, 2005; Pelz and Canosa, 2001) to their future-relevant location.
evidence: This is a hypothetical alternative scenario discussed in relation to prior literature.

claim: If memory contents were remapped, one would have expected to exclusively find a future-directed gaze bias.
source: However, in this case, one may have expected to exclusively find a future-directed gaze bias, unlike what we observed.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would be expected under the remapping hypothesis.

claim: There was no direct evidence for remapping in the period between encoding and cue.
source: Moreover, using a complementary analysis of saccade directions along the axis of the future rule (de Vries and van Ede, 2024), we found no direct evidence for remapping in the period between encoding and cue (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is supported by analysis shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: The brain simultaneously retains the copy of both past and future-relevant locations in working memory, and (re)activates each during mnemonic selection.
source: In contrast, our data suggest that the brain simultaneously retains the copy of both past and future-relevant locations in working memory, and (re)activates each during mnemonic selection.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: It is not surprising that the future location is considered.
source: Thus, while it is not surprising that the future location is considered (Hayhoe and Ballard, 2005; Pelz and Canosa, 2001; Mennie et al., 2007), it is far less trivial that both past and future attributes would be retained and (re)activated together.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work on anticipatory attention.

claim: It is far less trivial that both past and future attributes would be retained and (re)activated together.
source: Thus, while it is not surprising that the future location is considered (Hayhoe and Ballard, 2005; Pelz and Canosa, 2001; Mennie et al., 2007), it is far less trivial that both past and future attributes would be retained and (re)activated together.
evidence: This emphasizes the novelty of the joint consideration finding.

claim: The discrete nature of saccades enabled demonstration of truly joint consideration of past and future attributes at the single-trial level.
source: By capitalising on the discrete nature of saccades, we were able to demonstrate the truly joint consideration of past and future attributes, at the single-trial level.
evidence: This describes a methodological advantage that enabled the key finding.

claim: This approach bypasses a fundamental challenge of disentangling multiple potential single-trial interpretations when only having trial-average data available.
source: As such we were able to bypass a fundamental challenge of disentangling multiple potential single-trial interpretations when only having trial-average data available (for related discussions, see Stokes and Spaak, 2016; Jones, 2016; Nobre and van Ede, 2020).
evidence: This methodological point is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Microsaccades have important features that make them a promising complementary tool for uncovering the mechanisms of spatial attention.
source: Compared to the commonly used online indicator of spatial attention, such as electrophysiological measures, microsaccades have important features that make them a promising complementary tool for uncovering the mechanisms of spatial attention (Rolfs, 2009; Engbert, 2006), including when directed internally as we have shown here.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and the current study's findings.

claim: Microsaccades are discrete events, allowing to track spatial attention at the single-trial level.
source: First, as we have discussed above, microsaccades are discrete events, allowing to track spatial attention at the single-trial level.
evidence: This is a property of microsaccades that was exploited in the study.

claim: Microsaccades are not limited to tracking spatial attention toward the left or right visual field, as electrophysiology indicators often are.
source: Second, microsaccades are not limited to tracking spatial attention toward the left or right visual field, as electrophysiology indicators often are.
evidence: This is a methodological advantage of microsaccades compared to other measures.

claim: The past gaze bias replicates prior studies.
source: While the past gaze bias that we report here replicates our own prior studies (Liu et al., 2022a; van Ede et al., 2021; van Ede et al., 2019; van Ede et al., 2020), here we for the first time demonstrate a similar bias to the future-relevant memory location that is similarly driven by microsaccades.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work from the same lab.

claim: The study demonstrates for the first time a similar bias to the future-relevant memory location that is similarly driven by microsaccades.
source: While the past gaze bias that we report here replicates our own prior studies (Liu et al., 2022a; van Ede et al., 2021; van Ede et al., 2019; van Ede et al., 2020), here we for the first time demonstrate a similar bias to the future-relevant memory location that is similarly driven by microsaccades.
evidence: This is a novel finding of the current study.

claim: The future signal reflects either the selection of a future copy of the cued memory content or anticipatory attention to the anticipated location of its associated test-stimulus.
source: This signal may reflect either of two situations: the selection of a future copy of the cued memory content or anticipatory attention to the anticipated location of its associated test-stimulus.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of what the future bias might represent.

claim: The future signal should be considered a content-specific memory attribute because the two memory contents were always associated with opposite testing locations.
source: Either way, by the nature of our experimental design, this future signal should be considered a content-specific memory attribute for two reasons. First, the two memory contents were always associated with opposite testing locations, hence the observed bias to the relevant future location must be attributed specifically to the cued memory content.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the experimental design.

claim: The to-be-tested location was dependent on the item's encoding location, regardless of its colour.
source: Second, we cued which memory item would become tested based on its colour, but the to-be-tested location was dependent on the item's encoding location, regardless of its colour.
evidence: This describes a key aspect of the experimental design.

claim: Consideration of the item's future-relevant location must have been mediated by selecting the memory item itself.
source: Hence, consideration of the item's future-relevant location must have been mediated by selecting the memory item itself, as it could not have proceeded via cue colour directly.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the experimental design.

claim: The data reveal how the future feature can be accessed from memory together with the specific memory content that it is associated with.
source: Accordingly, our data reveal how this future feature can be accessed from memory together with the specific memory content that it is associated with, implying joint storage and utilisation of past and future memory attributes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: A critical difference with common pre-cue studies is that the cue in the current task never directly informed the relevant future location.
source: A critical difference with common pre-cue studies, however, is that the cue in our task never directly informed the relevant future location.
evidence: This describes a key distinction of the current experimental design.

claim: The future location was a feature of the cued memory item, not of the cue itself.
source: Rather, as also stressed above, the future location was a feature of the cued memory item (according to the future rule), and not of the cue itself.
evidence: This describes a key aspect of the experimental design.

claim: The past location of the memory items was technically irrelevant for the task and could thus, in principle, be dropped after encoding.
source: In our study, the past location of the memory items was technically irrelevant for the task and could thus, in principle, be dropped after encoding.
evidence: This is a logical observation about the task design.

claim: One possibility is that participants remapped the two memory items to their future locations soon after encoding, and had started – but not finished – dropping the past location by the time the cue arrived.
source: One possibility is that participants remapped the two memory items to their future locations soon after encoding, and had started – but not finished – dropping the past location by the time the cue arrived.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The past locations may be utilised by the brain to help individuate/separate the two memory items.
source: Alternatively, however, the past locations may be utilised by the brain to help individuate/separate the two memory items.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of why past locations might be retained.

claim: By storing items with regard to multiple spatial frames, memories may become more robust to decay and/or interference.
source: Moreover, by storing items with regard to multiple spatial frames (Draschkow et al., 2022) – here with regard to both past and future visual locations – it is conceivable that memories may become more robust to decay and/or interference.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation to related work.

claim: The data complement other recent studies investigating visual working memory in more dynamic contexts.
source: Our data complement other recent studies investigating visual working memory in more dynamic contexts (Brincat et al., 2021; van Ede et al., 2021; Draschkow et al., 2022; Chung et al., 2022; de Vries et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2022), and showcase the rich nature of working memory representations.
evidence: This contextualizes the findings within the broader literature.

claim: Recent studies have uncovered the joint consideration of allocentric and egocentric spatial frames for working memory.
source: For example, akin to our finding of joint consideration of past and future locations in working memory, recent studies have uncovered the joint consideration of allocentric and egocentric spatial frames for working memory (Draschkow et al., 2022; Fiehler et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The joint retention of multiple spatial attributes may make memories more robust, as well as more flexible for serving continuously evolving demands during everyday behaviour.
source: We speculate that the joint retention of multiple spatial attributes may make memories more robust, as well as more flexible for serving continuously evolving demands during everyday behaviour.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Sample size of 25 was determined a-priori based on previous publications from the lab with similar experimental designs.
source: Sample size of 25 was determined a-priori based on previous publications from the lab with similar experimental designs, and that relied on the same outcome measure (Liu et al., 2022a; van Ede et al., 2021; van Ede et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the rationale for sample size determination.

claim: Three participants were replaced due to chance-level performance.
source: To achieve the intended sample size, three participants were replaced due to chance-level performance.
evidence: This describes an aspect of data collection.

claim: The colour change served as a 100% valid retro-cue.
source: This colour change served as a 100% valid retro-cue, prompting participants to select the colour-matching target memory item.
evidence: This describes a key aspect of the experimental design.

claim: The study consisted of four sessions, each contained five blocks of 32 trials each.
source: In total, the study consisted of four sessions, each contained five blocks of 32 trials each.
evidence: This describes the experimental structure.

claim: The study lasted approximately 70 min per participant.
source: The study lasted approximately 70min per participant.
evidence: This describes the duration of the experiment.

claim: Gaze was tracked from a single eye using an EyeLink 1000 at a sampling rate of 1000Hz.
source: Gaze was tracked from a single eye (right eye in all participants except one for which the left eye provided a better signal) using an EyeLink 1000 (SR Research) at a sampling rate of 1000Hz.
evidence: This describes the eye-tracking methodology.

claim: A velocity-based method was employed to identify gaze shifts.
source: To identify gaze shifts, we employed a velocity-based method that we established in our prior studies (Liu et al., 2022a; Liu et al., 2022b), that builds on other velocity-based detection methods (e.g., Engbert and Kliegl, 2003).
evidence: This describes the saccade detection methodology.

claim: A cluster-based permutation approach was used to evaluate the reliability of patterns in the gaze data.
source: To evaluate the reliability of patterns in our gaze data, we used a cluster-based permutation approach (Maris and Oostenveld, 2007).
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis method.
